nodes.label: Self-attention
nodes.blurb: Every token looks at every other token and mixes in what it finds. The one idea everything else here builds on.

nodes.label: Multi-head attention
nodes.blurb: Several attention heads run in parallel, each looking for a different kind of relation.

nodes.label: MQA, GQA, MLA
nodes.blurb: Ways to share keys and values across heads so the KV cache gets smaller.

nodes.label: Sliding-window and sparse attention
nodes.blurb: Let each token look only at a window or a pattern of others, to cut the quadratic cost.

nodes.label: Linear attention and hybrids
nodes.blurb: Attention rewritten so its cost grows linearly, and models that mix it with the standard kind.

nodes.label: The Transformer: encoder and decoder
nodes.blurb: The 2017 design: an encoder that reads and a decoder that writes, built only from attention and small MLPs.

nodes.label: Position embeddings
nodes.blurb: Attention has no sense of order, so a learned vector per position is added to every token.

nodes.label: BERT
nodes.blurb: A Transformer encoder that reads text in both directions, pre-trained once and fine-tuned for any task.

nodes.label: Masked language modelling
nodes.blurb: Hide 15% of the words and train the model to guess them from both sides.

nodes.label: Pre-train, then fine-tune
nodes.blurb: Train once on a huge dataset, then adapt a copy to each task with one small new layer.

nodes.label: The [CLS] / [class] token
nodes.blurb: An extra token whose output vector stands for the whole input. BERT invented it; ViT reused it.

nodes.label: Vision Transformer (ViT)
nodes.blurb: Cut a picture into 16×16 patches, treat them as words, and feed them to an unchanged Transformer encoder.

nodes.label: Images as patches
nodes.blurb: A 224×224 picture becomes 196 patches of 768 numbers each: the image's tokens.

nodes.label: Inductive bias versus data
nodes.blurb: Built-in assumptions help with little data; with 300 million images, learning from data wins.

nodes.label: Convolutional networks (ResNet)
nodes.blurb: The design that ruled computer vision from 2012 to 2020: small filters slid across the picture, with residual shortcuts.

nodes.label: Prefill and decode
nodes.blurb: How an LLM answers: read the whole prompt at once, then write one token at a time.

nodes.label: KV cache
nodes.blurb: The keys and values of every past token, kept in memory so they are not recomputed. It is the biggest memory bill.

nodes.label: vLLM: paging and batching
nodes.blurb: Serving thousands of requests by paging the KV cache like an operating system and batching continuously.

nodes.label: Speculative decoding
nodes.blurb: A small model drafts several tokens; the big model checks them in one step. Same words, fewer steps.

nodes.label: RAG
nodes.blurb: Retrieve the right passages first, then let the model answer from them. A full book, from first principles.

nodes.label: Embeddings
nodes.blurb: Meaning as geometry: texts become vectors, and similar meanings land close together.

nodes.label: Vector search and HNSW
nodes.blurb: Finding the nearest vectors among millions fast, with a layered graph of neighbours.

nodes.label: BM25 and hybrid search
nodes.blurb: Keyword scores and vector scores, fused, beat either alone.

nodes.label: Rerankers
nodes.blurb: A second, slower model (often BERT-like) re-orders the top results more carefully.

nodes.label: Evaluating RAG
nodes.blurb: Every retrieval and generation metric, and how to measure a pipeline honestly.

nodes.label: LangGraph and agentic RAG
nodes.blurb: RAG as a graph of steps that can loop, branch and call tools.

nodes.label: Multi-agent systems and guardrails
nodes.blurb: Several agents working together, and the checks that keep them in bounds.

nodes.label: Jev: a model that decides
nodes.blurb: A video on an AI model that does not talk, it decides.

nodes.label: Why GPUs exist
nodes.blurb: Thousands of simple cores doing the same arithmetic at once: exactly what matrix multiplication needs.

nodes.label: The CUDA programming model
nodes.blurb: Threads, blocks and grids: how work is handed to a GPU.

nodes.label: CPU parallelism
nodes.blurb: What a CPU can and cannot do in parallel, and why that is not enough.
